questions.text: I should be able to please everybody.
My value as a person depends greatly on what others think of me.
If I fail at something, it means I'm a failure as a person.
I must be perfect at everything I do.
If something bad happens once, it will likely happen again.
When something goes wrong, I expect the worst possible outcome.
Things are either completely good or completely bad.
If I'm not a complete success, I'm a failure.
People should always follow the rules.
I frequently use words like 'must', 'should', and 'have to' when thinking about myself and others.
If I feel anxious, there must be something to be afraid of.
If I feel sad, it must mean that something bad has happened.
When bad things happen, it's usually my fault.
I take responsibility for things outside my control.
I need other people's approval to feel good about myself.
I can't stand making mistakes.
If one bad thing happens, everything will fall apart.
People are either with me or against me.
Others should always meet my expectations.
My feelings accurately reflect reality.
When a group project fails, it's probably because of my contribution.
Criticism means that I've done something wrong.
If I don't set the highest standards for myself, I'll end up a second-rate person.
Small problems will snowball into big ones if I don't solve them immediately.
Either I do something perfectly or not at all.
There is a right way to do everything.
If I feel guilty, I must have done something wrong.
When someone is upset, it's probably because of something I did or said.

perfectionism.name: Perfectionism
perfectionism.description: The belief that you must be perfect in everything you do. This attitude sets unrealistically high standards and can lead to self-criticism when these standards aren't met.
perfectionism.highScoreDescription: You have a strong tendency toward perfectionism. You set extremely high standards for yourself and may be highly self-critical when you don't meet these standards. This can lead to procrastination, anxiety, and avoidance of challenges.
perfectionism.averageScoreDescription: You show some perfectionist tendencies. While you value doing things well, you may sometimes set standards that are difficult to achieve, which can cause stress or disappointment.
perfectionism.lowScoreDescription: You have a healthy approach to achievement. You strive to do well but accept that perfection isn't always possible or necessary. This balanced perspective allows you to take on challenges without excessive self-pressure.
improvementTips: Set realistic and achievable goals
Practice self-compassion when you make mistakes
Focus on progress rather than perfection
Celebrate small wins and improvements

need_for_approval.name: Need for Approval
need_for_approval.description: The belief that your worth depends on what others think of you. This attitude places excessive importance on gaining approval and avoiding rejection from others.
need_for_approval.highScoreDescription: You have a strong need for others' approval. You may often worry about what others think of you and base your self-worth largely on external validation. This can make you vulnerable to rejection and criticism.
need_for_approval.averageScoreDescription: You sometimes seek validation from others. While you value others' opinions, you don't completely base your self-worth on their approval.
need_for_approval.lowScoreDescription: You have a healthy sense of self-worth that isn't overly dependent on others' approval. You can consider others' feedback without letting it define your value as a person.
improvementTips: Practice self-validation and self-acceptance
Set boundaries in relationships
Identify your core values independent of others' opinions
Challenge thoughts that link your worth to others' approval

catastrophic_thinking.name: Catastrophic Thinking
catastrophic_thinking.description: The tendency to expect the worst possible outcomes. This attitude involves magnifying negative events and minimizing positive ones.
catastrophic_thinking.highScoreDescription: You have a strong tendency toward catastrophic thinking. You often anticipate the worst possible outcomes and may overestimate the likelihood of negative events. This can lead to excessive worry and anxiety.
catastrophic_thinking.averageScoreDescription: You sometimes engage in catastrophic thinking. While you may occasionally expect negative outcomes, you don't consistently assume the worst will happen.
catastrophic_thinking.lowScoreDescription: You generally maintain a balanced perspective on potential outcomes. You can realistically assess situations without automatically assuming the worst.
improvementTips: Practice evidence-based thinking
Consider multiple possible outcomes, not just the worst
Use probability thinking instead of possibility thinking
Focus on what you can control

dichotomous_thinking.name: Black-and-White Thinking
dichotomous_thinking.description: The tendency to see things in absolute, all-or-nothing terms. This attitude leaves no room for middle ground or nuance.
dichotomous_thinking.highScoreDescription: You have a strong tendency toward black-and-white thinking. You often categorize experiences, people, or outcomes as entirely good or entirely bad, with little room for middle ground. This can lead to extreme judgments and emotional reactions.
dichotomous_thinking.averageScoreDescription: You sometimes engage in black-and-white thinking. While you may occasionally see things in absolute terms, you can also recognize nuance in many situations.
dichotomous_thinking.lowScoreDescription: You generally think in nuanced ways. You recognize that most situations, people, and experiences contain both positive and negative aspects, which allows for balanced assessments.
improvementTips: Look for the gray areas in situations
Use a scale (1-10) instead of absolute categories
Practice using 'both/and' instead of 'either/or' thinking
Identify the spectrum of possibilities between extremes

demandingness.name: Rigid Rules and Demands
demandingness.description: The belief that things should or must be a certain way. This attitude involves inflexible expectations about yourself, others, and the world.
demandingness.highScoreDescription: You have a strong tendency toward rigid rules and demands. You often use words like 'should,' 'must,' and 'have to' when thinking about yourself and others. This inflexibility can lead to frustration and disappointment when reality doesn't match your expectations.
demandingness.averageScoreDescription: You sometimes hold rigid expectations. While you have certain standards and preferences, you can also be flexible when necessary.
demandingness.lowScoreDescription: You generally maintain flexible expectations. You can adapt to changing circumstances and accept when things don't go as planned, which promotes resilience and reduces unnecessary stress.
improvementTips: Replace 'should' statements with preferences
Practice acceptance of things you cannot change
Distinguish between ideals and requirements
Develop flexibility in your expectations

emotional_reasoning.name: Emotional Reasoning
emotional_reasoning.description: The belief that your feelings reflect reality. This attitude involves treating emotions as evidence for the truth, regardless of contradictory rational evidence.
emotional_reasoning.highScoreDescription: You have a strong tendency toward emotional reasoning. You often assume that your feelings accurately reflect reality, which can lead to conclusions that aren't supported by objective evidence. This can reinforce negative thought patterns.
emotional_reasoning.averageScoreDescription: You sometimes engage in emotional reasoning. While you may occasionally let your feelings guide your interpretations, you can also step back and consider objective evidence.
emotional_reasoning.lowScoreDescription: You generally distinguish between feelings and facts. You recognize that emotions, while important, don't always accurately reflect reality, which allows for more balanced assessments of situations.
improvementTips: Distinguish between feelings and facts
Ask 'What's the evidence?' when making interpretations
Consider alternative explanations for your emotions
Practice mindful awareness of emotions without judgment

personalization.name: Personalization and Blame
personalization.description: The tendency to take excessive responsibility for external events. This attitude involves blaming yourself for things that are outside your control or only partially your responsibility.
personalization.highScoreDescription: You have a strong tendency toward personalization and self-blame. You often assume responsibility for negative events that may be outside your control or only partially your responsibility. This can lead to excessive guilt and self-criticism.
personalization.averageScoreDescription: You sometimes personalize external events. While you may occasionally blame yourself unnecessarily, you can also recognize when factors beyond your control contribute to outcomes.
personalization.lowScoreDescription: You generally maintain a balanced view of responsibility. You can acknowledge your role in situations without taking on excessive blame, which promotes healthy accountability.
improvementTips: Identify all factors that contribute to outcomes
Distinguish between responsibility and blame
Practice self-compassion when things go wrong
Consider what you'd tell a friend in the same situation

high.name: High Dysfunctional Attitudes
high.description: Your responses indicate a high level of dysfunctional attitudes. These thought patterns may significantly impact your emotions and behaviors, potentially contributing to stress, anxiety, or low mood.
high.improvementFocus: Working on cognitive restructuring techniques to challenge and modify these thought patterns would be beneficial. Consider exploring resources on cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) or mindfulness-based approaches.

average.name: Moderate Dysfunctional Attitudes
average.description: Your responses indicate a moderate level of dysfunctional attitudes. While you show some healthy thinking patterns, there are specific areas where your thoughts may become unhelpful.
average.improvementFocus: Focus on the specific attitude types where you scored highest, and practice awareness of these patterns in your daily life. Small adjustments to these thinking habits can lead to significant improvements in well-being.

low.name: Low Dysfunctional Attitudes
low.description: Your responses indicate a low level of dysfunctional attitudes. You generally maintain healthy and flexible thinking patterns, which is beneficial for emotional well-being.
low.improvementFocus: Continue to nurture your healthy thinking patterns. Consider sharing your strategies with others or exploring ways to further enhance your emotional resilience and mental flexibility.
